posts.content:

Not every family lives on base. Waitlists, family size, pets, or simply wanting more space can lead you to the off-base rental market. Finding the right home from hundreds or thousands of miles away, often on a tight PCS timeline, takes a smart approach.

Start With the Housing Service Office

Every installation has a housing office that helps with both on-base and off-base housing. They can tell you about waitlist times, neighborhoods that are popular with military families, typical commute times, and landlords with complaints on file. Contact them as soon as you have orders. Many installations also list rentals on the DoD’s official Automated Housing Referral Network (AHRN.com).

Know Your Budget

Look up your BAH rate first, then set a total monthly budget that includes utilities, internet, and renters insurance. Our guide BAH Explained breaks down how the allowance works.

Choose the Right Neighborhood

  • Commute: check drive times to the gate you will actually use, at rush hour.
  • Schools: if you have children, research schools by address, since assignment boundaries can split neighborhoods.
  • Safety: look at local crime maps and talk to people who live there.
  • Amenities: grocery stores, parks, gyms, and medical care.

Avoid Rental Scams

Military families are frequent scam targets because they often rent sight unseen. Watch out for:

  • Rent that is far below market for the area
  • A “landlord” who is out of the country and cannot show the home
  • Requests to pay by wire transfer, gift cards, or payment apps before you have a lease
  • Pressure to sign or pay immediately

Verify ownership through county property records, ask for a live video tour, and never send money before seeing a lease. The housing office can help you check a listing.

Ask the Right Questions

  • Does the lease include a military clause?
  • What utilities are included?
  • What is the pet policy and pet deposit?
  • Who handles maintenance, and how fast?
  • Is renters insurance required?

Remember that the SCRA lets you terminate a lease if you receive PCS or qualifying deployment orders. Read our SCRA lease guide before you sign.

Get Renters Insurance

Renters insurance is affordable and covers your belongings if there is a fire, theft, or water damage. Keep an inventory of your belongings on your phone or in a home inventory notebook. It also makes household goods claims easier after a PCS.

Make Moving In Easier

Off-base rentals do not always come with the extras that on-base homes do. Depending on the home, you may want window AC units, a washer and dryer if hookups are available but appliances are not, or a mesh Wi-Fi system for a bigger house. Ask the landlord what is included before you buy.

posts.title: PCSing With Pets: Pet Policies, Paperwork, and Pet-Friendly Military Housing
posts.content:
Disclosure: Some links in this article are affiliate links. As an Amazon Associate, Military Housing Rentals earns from qualifying purchases, at no extra cost to you.

For many military families, pets are part of the family, and they PCS too. Moving a dog or cat across the country (or overseas) takes planning, especially when it comes to finding pet-friendly housing at your new duty station.

Know the Base Housing Pet Policy

Most privatized on-base housing communities welcome pets, but almost all have rules. Common policies include:

  • A limit on the number of pets per household, often two
  • Restrictions on certain dog breeds and on exotic animals
  • Required vaccinations and pet registration with the installation veterinary clinic
  • Microchipping requirements on many installations
  • Leash and waste-cleanup rules in common areas

Policies differ by service, installation, and housing company, so contact the housing office at your gaining base before you move. If your pet is not allowed on base, you will need to look for off-base military housing rentals that accept pets.

Prepare Your Pet’s Paperwork

  • Up-to-date vaccination records, including rabies
  • A health certificate from a veterinarian, if required by your airline or destination
  • Microchip number and registration details
  • Recent photos of your pet in case they get lost

For overseas moves, requirements can take months. Start early and check the destination country’s rules, the USDA APHIS pet travel guidance, and your installation veterinary treatment facility.

Gear That Makes Pet Travel Easier

  • An airline-compliant pet carrier or a hard-sided travel crate sized so your pet can stand and turn around
  • A collapsible travel water bowl for road trips
  • A dog car seat cover to protect your vehicle
  • A GPS pet tracker in case your pet slips away in an unfamiliar place
  • An ID tag with your cell phone number

Get your pet used to the crate weeks before the move by feeding meals in it and taking short drives.

On Moving Day

Packing and loading days are stressful for animals: strangers, noise, and open doors. Board your pet, leave them with a friend, or keep them in a closed room with a sign on the door. Pack a bag with food, medication, leash, waste bags, and a favorite toy or blanket that rides with you.

Settling In at Your New Home

  • Pet-proof the house before letting your pet explore. Check fences and gates for gaps.
  • Register your pet with the installation veterinary clinic if required.
  • Update your pet’s microchip with your new address and phone number.
  • Keep routines consistent: same feeding times and walks help your pet adjust faster.

Protect Your Deposit

Pet damage is one of the most common move-out charges. Use washable furniture covers, keep nails trimmed, and clean accidents quickly with an enzyme pet stain cleaner. See our inspection tips for more ways to protect your deposit.

Plan Ahead

With a little preparation, your pets can PCS as smoothly as the rest of the family. Use our PCS moving checklist to keep the whole move on track, and browse military housing rentals near your new duty station.

posts.title: 8 Renter-Friendly Upgrades to Make Base Housing Feel Like Home
posts.content:
Disclosure: Some links in this article are affiliate links. As an Amazon Associate, Military Housing Rentals earns from qualifying purchases, at no extra cost to you.

Base housing and military rentals come with rules: no painting without permission, limits on nail holes, and a move-out inspection waiting at the end. But that does not mean your house has to feel temporary. With a few renter-friendly upgrades, you can make any set of quarters feel like home and take everything with you at your next PCS.

1. Lighting That Changes the Mood

Military housing often comes with basic overhead fixtures. Warm lamps make a huge difference. Try plug-in wall sconces that need no hardwiring, smart LED bulbs you can dim from your phone, or under-cabinet LED light bars for a dark kitchen.

2. Wall Decor Without the Damage

Use picture-hanging strips for lightweight frames, or lean a large floor mirror against the wall to brighten a room. A peel-and-stick wallpaper accent wall can add personality, but check your housing office’s rules and test a small spot first.

3. Rugs to Warm Up Hard Floors

Many newer base homes have vinyl plank floors. A good washable area rug adds warmth, reduces noise, and protects the floor. Add a non-slip rug pad so it stays put.

4. Curtains and Blackout Shades

Housing-issued blinds are functional but rarely pretty. A tension curtain rod needs no drilling, and blackout curtains are a must for shift workers and kids’ rooms.

5. Storage That Moves With You

Closet space varies wildly from one base to the next. Freestanding storage adapts to any floor plan: cube storage organizers, over-the-door organizers, and under-bed storage bins all pack flat or double as moving containers.

6. Kitchen Upgrades

Swap in drawer organizers, add a rolling kitchen cart for extra counter space, and use shelf risers to double cabinet space.

7. A Military Family Command Center

Deployments, school schedules, and PCS deadlines are easier when everyone can see them. A magnetic dry-erase calendar on the fridge or a wall-mounted mail and key organizer by the door keeps your household on track.

8. Outdoor Space

Many on-base homes include a patio or fenced yard. Solar string lights, a few folding patio chairs, and self-watering planters turn it into an extra room. Check your community’s yard rules before adding anything permanent.

Before You Upgrade: Check the Rules

Every privatized housing company and landlord has its own policies. Before making changes, ask the housing office what is allowed and get approvals in writing. When it is time to leave, return everything to its original condition. Our move-in and move-out inspection guide covers what inspectors look for.

posts.title: Move-In and Move-Out Inspection Tips for Military Housing
posts.content:
Disclosure: Some links in this article are affiliate links. As an Amazon Associate, Military Housing Rentals earns from qualifying purchases, at no extra cost to you.

Your move-in and move-out inspections can be the difference between getting your full deposit back and paying for damage you never caused. Whether you are moving into privatized base housing or an off-base rental, a careful inspection protects you.

Why Inspections Matter So Much for Military Families

Military families move more often than most renters, and the timing is rarely flexible. You may be clearing quarters with movers in the driveway or signing for a new home after a long cross-country drive. That is exactly when details get missed. A system makes it quick.

Move-In Inspection Checklist

Do this before the household goods arrive, while rooms are empty and everything is visible.

Walls, Floors, and Ceilings

  • Holes, nail pops, scuffs, and paint touch-ups
  • Carpet stains, burns, and loose seams
  • Scratches or water damage on hard floors
  • Ceiling stains that could signal past leaks

Kitchen and Appliances

  • Run the dishwasher, oven, stovetop burners, microwave, and garbage disposal
  • Check the refrigerator temperature and ice maker
  • Look under the sink for leaks or mold

Bathrooms

  • Flush toilets and check for running water
  • Look for cracked tiles, worn caulk, and slow drains
  • Run the exhaust fan

Safety and Systems

  • Test smoke and carbon monoxide detectors
  • Run heating and air conditioning
  • Locate the breaker panel and main water shut-off
  • Check that windows lock and screens are intact

Document Everything

Take wide shots of each room plus close-ups of every defect, and keep a written list that matches your photos. Email the photos to yourself or the housing office so there is a dated record. A small tape measure in close-up photos shows the size of a stain or scratch, and a bright rechargeable flashlight helps you spot problems in closets and under sinks.

Submit your list to the property manager within the deadline they give you, often a few days after move-in, and keep a copy.

During Your Stay

Report maintenance issues quickly and in writing through the work order system. Small leaks become big repairs. A record of work orders also shows you reported problems rather than caused them.

Simple renter-friendly habits help too: felt furniture pads protect floors, removable adhesive hooks reduce nail holes, and a doormat and boot tray keep carpets cleaner.

Move-Out Inspection Checklist

  • Ask for the cleaning standard in writing, and ask if there is a pre-inspection you can schedule.
  • Patch small nail holes with spackle and a putty knife if your lease allows it.
  • Deep-clean the oven, refrigerator, bathroom grout, baseboards, and window tracks. A magic eraser sponge pack handles scuffs on walls and doors.
  • Replace burned-out light bulbs and HVAC filters.
  • Remove all trash and personal items, including from the garage, sheds, and the yard.
  • Photograph every room after cleaning, using the same angles as your move-in photos.

If You Disagree With Charges

Ask for an itemized list of charges, compare it to your move-in report and photos, and dispute anything that was pre-existing or normal wear and tear. For privatized base housing, the installation housing office and resident advocates can help. For off-base rentals, your legal assistance office can explain your state’s security deposit laws.

Ready for Your Next Home?

Take your time with the inspection and you will start your next assignment without surprises. Browse our military housing rentals and keep our PCS moving checklist handy for the rest of your move.

posts.title: Breaking a Lease on PCS Orders: The SCRA and Military Clauses Explained
posts.content:
Disclosure: Some links in this article are affiliate links. As an Amazon Associate, Military Housing Rentals earns from qualifying purchases, at no extra cost to you.

Orders can arrive at the worst possible time, like six months into a twelve-month lease. Fortunately, federal law gives service members a way out. The Servicemembers Civil Relief Act (SCRA) lets you terminate a residential lease early without penalty in specific situations.

This guide explains who qualifies, how to give proper notice, and what to watch out for. It is general information, not legal advice. Your installation’s legal assistance office can review your situation for free.

Who Can Terminate a Lease Under the SCRA?

Under 50 U.S.C. § 3955, you can generally terminate a residential lease if:

  • You signed the lease before entering military service and then entered active duty, or
  • You signed the lease while on active duty and then received PCS orders, or
  • You signed the lease while on active duty and then received orders to deploy with a unit for 90 days or more.

Protections can also extend to leases signed by a dependent in certain cases, and to the surviving spouse of a service member who dies while on active duty. Read the full text of the law at the Department of Justice SCRA page.

How to Terminate Your Lease Correctly

  1. Write a notice stating that you are terminating the lease under the SCRA.
  2. Attach a copy of your orders or a letter from your commanding officer.
  3. Deliver it by hand (get a signed receipt), by a private carrier, or by certified mail with return receipt. Keep copies of everything.

Keep a copy of the notice and receipt in your PCS folder. If you do not have a printer, a compact all-in-one home printer and scanner is worth having in a military household; you will be printing and scanning orders constantly.

When Does the Termination Take Effect?

For a lease with monthly rent, termination is effective 30 days after the next rent due date following delivery of your notice. For example, if rent is due on the 1st and you deliver notice on June 10, the next due date is July 1 and termination takes effect July 31. You owe rent through that date.

What the Landlord Can and Cannot Do

  • The landlord cannot charge an early termination fee or penalty for a lawful SCRA termination.
  • The landlord must refund any rent you paid in advance for the period after termination, generally within 30 days.
  • The landlord can still deduct for unpaid rent before termination and for damage beyond normal wear and tear, as the lease and state law allow.

Military Clauses vs. the SCRA

Many landlords near bases include a military clause in their leases. These often mirror the SCRA, but some add extra conditions, like requiring that you move a certain distance away. The SCRA sets a federal minimum that a lease cannot take away, so if a military clause is less favorable, the SCRA still applies. Read every clause before you sign.

Protect Your Security Deposit

Terminating legally does not guarantee your deposit back. Document the home’s condition at move-out with dated photos and video, and attend the final walkthrough if you can. See our move-in and move-out inspection tips for a full checklist.

Choose Military-Friendly Housing Next Time

One way to avoid lease headaches entirely is to rent from communities that work with military families every day. Privatized on-base housing and many military housing rentals are built around PCS timelines. If you are weighing your options, our article on renting vs. buying for military families can help.

posts.title: BAH Explained: How the Military Housing Allowance Works
posts.content:
Disclosure: Some links in this article are affiliate links. As an Amazon Associate, Military Housing Rentals earns from qualifying purchases, at no extra cost to you.

Basic Allowance for Housing (BAH) is one of the most important parts of military pay, and one of the most misunderstood. It decides how much you can comfortably spend on rent, whether on-base or off-base housing makes more sense, and how far your budget stretches at a new duty station.

Here is a plain-English explanation of how BAH works and how to use it when choosing a rental.

What Is BAH?

BAH is a U.S.-based allowance that helps service members pay for housing when government quarters are not provided. It is paid monthly, it is not taxable, and it is meant to cover most of the cost of renting a typical home in your area plus average utilities.

What Determines Your BAH Rate?

Three factors set your rate:

  • Duty station location: rates are set by military housing area, based on the ZIP code of your permanent duty station, not where you choose to live.
  • Pay grade: higher pay grades receive a higher allowance.
  • Dependency status: members with dependents receive the “with dependents” rate, regardless of how many dependents they have.

You can look up your exact rate with the official BAH rate lookup from the Defense Travel Management Office. New rates take effect each January 1.

Rate Protection

If BAH rates in your area go down while you stay at the same duty station, individual rate protection generally keeps you at the higher rate you were already receiving. If rates go up, you get the increase. Rate protection ends when you PCS, get promoted into a new rate, or change dependency status, so always check your new rate before signing a lease.

How BAH Works With On-Base Housing

In privatized on-base housing, your BAH typically goes directly to the housing company as rent through an allotment, and in most communities it covers rent and a baseline amount of utilities. That predictability is one reason many families choose to live on base. Learn more in our guide: What Is Base Housing?

Using BAH to Rent Off Base

If you live off base, you receive BAH in your paycheck and pay rent yourself. You are allowed to spend more or less than your BAH. Living below your allowance is a common way military families build savings, while spending more might get you a bigger home or a shorter commute.

When you compare off-base rentals, add up the full cost:

  • Monthly rent
  • Electric, gas, water, sewer, and trash
  • Internet
  • Renters insurance
  • Commute costs (fuel, tolls, extra wear on your vehicle)
  • Deposits and pet fees

A Simple BAH Budgeting Rule

Many families aim to keep rent plus utilities at or below their BAH. That way base pay can go toward food, savings, and debt. A simple monthly budget planner or personal finance book for military families can help you build the habit, especially in the first months after a move when expenses pile up.

Other Housing Allowances to Know

  • OHA (Overseas Housing Allowance): for members stationed overseas and living in private housing.
  • TLE (Temporary Lodging Expense): helps cover hotel costs during a CONUS PCS.
  • TLA (Temporary Lodging Allowance): the overseas version of TLE.
  • DLA (Dislocation Allowance): a one-time payment to help with moving costs.

Ask your finance office which allowances apply to your move. Rules change, and the official sources are always the final word.

The Bottom Line

BAH is designed to make housing affordable wherever you are stationed. Know your rate, compare total monthly costs, and decide whether on-base convenience or off-base flexibility fits your family better. Then browse our military housing rental listings to see what is available near your base.

posts.title: PCS Moving Checklist: A Step-by-Step Guide for Military Families
posts.content:
Disclosure: Some links in this article are affiliate links. As an Amazon Associate, Military Housing Rentals earns from qualifying purchases, at no extra cost to you.

A permanent change of station is one of the biggest logistical projects a military family takes on. Between the household goods shipment, clearing quarters, school records, and finding a place to live at the new duty station, it is easy for something important to slip through the cracks.

This PCS moving checklist breaks the move into phases so you always know what to do next. Print it, share it with your spouse, and check items off as you go.

As Soon as You Have Orders

  • Get several copies of your orders (paper and PDF). Movers, landlords, schools, and utility companies will ask for them.
  • Schedule your household goods move through Move.mil as early as possible. Summer peak season fills up fast.
  • Contact the Housing Service Office (HSO) at your gaining installation to get on the on-base housing waitlist or request off-base referrals.
  • If you rent off base now, give your landlord written notice with a copy of your orders. Read our guide to breaking a lease with the SCRA.
  • Start a PCS binder or folder for orders, receipts, medical and school records, pet records, and inventory sheets. A document organizer with tabs keeps everything in one place.

Six to Eight Weeks Out

  • Declutter. Every pound counts against your weight allowance, and a lighter shipment is easier to unpack.
  • Take photos or video of every room and high-value item before the movers arrive. This makes claims far easier if something is damaged.
  • Request school records and immunization records for children, and look up schools near your new duty station.
  • Book pet travel and confirm airline or destination requirements for vaccinations and health certificates.
  • Research neighborhoods and military housing rentals near your new base.

Two to Four Weeks Out

  • Pack a do-not-pack area. Mark it clearly with bright do-not-pack labels or tape so movers skip it.
  • Set aside items you will carry yourself: IDs, passports, orders, jewelry, firearms (follow transport laws), prescriptions, and laptops.
  • Schedule utility shut-off at your current home and set-up at your new address.
  • Forward your mail with USPS and update your address with banks, insurance, and DFAS through myPay.
  • If you are doing a partial or full personally procured move (PPM), get heavy-duty moving boxes, packing tape with a dispenser, and moving blankets, and save every weight ticket and receipt.

Pack Day and Load Day

  • Be home and available. Walk the crew through the house and point out fragile or high-value items.
  • Check the inventory sheets carefully. Descriptions like “scratched” or “dented” written on everything can make claims harder later. Speak up if you disagree.
  • Keep kids and pets in a separate room or with a sitter.
  • Do a final walkthrough of every closet, cabinet, attic, and shed before the truck leaves.

Your Open-the-First-Night Box

Pack one bin per person that rides in your car. When the truck is late (and it often is), this box turns a hotel or empty house into something livable:

  • Sheets, pillows, and towels, or an air mattress with a built-in pump if you will arrive before your furniture
  • Toilet paper, paper towels, soap, and a basic cleaning supply kit
  • Phone chargers and a portable power bank
  • A small tool kit for reassembling furniture
  • Paper plates, cups, a pot, and simple snacks
  • Medications, a first aid kit, and copies of orders

Clearing Quarters

If you lived in base housing, schedule your pre-inspection and final inspection early. Ask exactly what the cleaning standard is, and photograph each room after you clean. Our move-in and move-out inspection guide walks through what inspectors usually look for.

At Your New Duty Station

  • Sign in and check in with the housing office.
  • Do a careful move-in inspection and document existing damage before you unpack.
  • Be present for delivery, check off every inventory number, and note damage on the delivery paperwork before signing.
  • File any claims within the deadlines given by your transportation service provider.
  • Update vehicle registration, driver’s license, and voter registration as required by your new state.

Final Thoughts

A PCS never goes exactly to plan, but a checklist turns chaos into a series of manageable tasks. Start early, keep your documents together, and lean on your installation’s relocation assistance program. When you are ready to look for a home, browse our current military housing listings or read what base housing is and how it works.

posts.title: What Is Base Housing?
posts.content:
Disclosure: Some links in this article are affiliate links. As an Amazon Associate, Military Housing Rentals earns from qualifying purchases, at no extra cost to you.

If you’re facing orders, planning a PCS, or simply trying to decide where your next home should be, one question comes up fast: what is base housing, and is it the right move for you?

Base housing—also called on-base housing—is one of the most talked-about options in military life. Some families love it. Others prefer living off base. The right choice depends on timing, lifestyle, family size, and financial priorities. I’ve seen service members rush into a decision simply because it felt familiar, and others hesitate because of outdated assumptions.

This guide cuts through the noise. No fluff. No myths repeated without context. Just clear answers, practical insight, and real-world considerations so you can decide with confidence.

What Is Base Housing?

At its core, base housing refers to residential homes located on or near a military installation and designated for active-duty service members and their families. These homes are typically managed either directly by the military or by private companies through public-private partnerships.

So when someone asks, what is base housing, the simplest answer is this:
It’s housing provided as part of military infrastructure to support readiness, stability, and community.

Unlike civilian rentals, base housing is deeply tied to military life. Your rank, dependency status, and duty station influence availability. Your housing allowance often flows directly into rent. And your neighbors? Almost always fellow service members or military families.

That changes the experience in important ways.

Why Base Housing Exists

Base housing wasn’t created for convenience alone. It exists to solve specific problems unique to military service.

  • Frequent relocations
  • Remote or high-cost duty stations
  • Unpredictable schedules
  • Deployment cycles

Living close to work reduces commute time, increases unit readiness, and gives families access to on-base services like schools, medical care, and child development centers.

In short, base housing is designed to reduce friction during already demanding transitions.

Who Is Eligible for Base Housing?

Eligibility is straightforward, but priority is not.

Generally, base housing is available to:

  • Active-duty service members with dependents
  • Some unaccompanied service members (depending on rank and availability)
  • Certain Guard or Reserve members on extended active orders

Priority is usually given based on:

  1. Rank
  2. Family size
  3. Availability at the installation
  4. Date of application

Single junior enlisted members often live in barracks rather than family housing, while higher ranks and larger families receive priority for detached homes or townhouses.

Timing matters. Applying early can make the difference between moving right in or waiting months.

How Base Housing Works in Practice

Once orders are issued, service members can apply for base housing through the installation’s housing office or online portal. You’ll submit:

  • Orders
  • Dependency information
  • Desired move-in date

From there, you’re placed on a waiting list. Some bases move fast. Others don’t.

Assignments depend on what’s available when your name reaches the top. You usually don’t choose a specific house, but you may be offered options within a neighborhood or housing category.

Once accepted, you sign a housing agreement—not a traditional lease—and move in.

Types of Base Housing You’ll See

Base housing is not one-size-fits-all. Housing stock varies widely by installation.

Common options include:

  • Single-family homes – Often for senior enlisted and officers
  • Townhomes or duplexes – Common for mid-grade families
  • Apartments – More typical at urban or overseas installations

Some neighborhoods feature older homes with generous layouts. Others offer newly built or renovated units with modern finishes.

Age of housing matters. So does renovation history. Always ask.

What’s Included When You Live in Base Housing?

This is where base housing becomes attractive for many families.

Most base housing includes:

  • Rent covered by BAH
  • Utilities (often all, sometimes capped)
  • Maintenance and emergency repairs
  • Lawn care and exterior upkeep
  • Access to playgrounds and community centers

No surprise repair bills. No negotiating with landlords. And no juggling multiple utility accounts.

That predictability matters, especially during high-tempo assignments.

How Much Does Base Housing Cost?

Here’s the key financial point:
Most base housing communities collect 100% of your Basic Allowance for Housing (BAH) as rent.

That means:

  • You don’t pay rent out of pocket
  • You don’t keep leftover BAH
  • Costs are fixed and predictable

This can be a win in high-cost areas. In lower-cost markets, living off base may allow you to pocket savings.

Here’s a simple comparison:

The math isn’t just monthly. It’s about time, stress, and long-term planning.

Pros of Living in Base Housing

There’s a reason many families choose base housing again and again.

Key advantages include:

  • Short commutes and predictable schedules
  • Strong sense of community
  • On-base schools, childcare, and services nearby
  • Easier transitions during PCS moves

For new service members or families with young children, base housing can simplify life during demanding seasons.

I’ve seen families regain hours each week simply by cutting a commute from 45 minutes to five.

Cons You Should Consider Honestly

Base housing isn’t perfect. And pretending otherwise leads to frustration.

Common drawbacks include:

  • Long waiting lists at popular installations
  • Limited customization or renovation options
  • Regular inspections
  • Strict rules around landscaping, parking, and modifications

You’re trading flexibility for convenience. For some, that’s an easy trade. For others, it’s a dealbreaker.

Base Housing vs Living Off Base

This decision deserves real thought.

Base housing works best for:

  • Families new to a duty station
  • Those prioritizing convenience and stability
  • Short-term assignments

Off-base housing often suits:

  • Families seeking more space or customization
  • Those wanting to build equity or save BAH
  • Long-term assignments in affordable markets

There’s no universal right answer. But there is a right answer for you.

Rules, Inspections, and Expectations

Living in base housing comes with structure.

Expect:

  • Routine inspections
  • Clear maintenance standards
  • Pet limits and breed restrictions
  • Guest and parking regulations

These rules exist to maintain community standards, but they can feel restrictive if you’re used to private rentals.

Ask for the resident handbook before committing. Always.

Practical Tips Before You Decide

Before choosing base housing, do this:

  • Tour multiple neighborhoods if possible
  • Ask current residents about maintenance response times
  • Compare off-base rentals using real numbers, not estimates
  • Consider your assignment length and family needs

And don’t rush. Housing decisions shape daily life more than almost anything else during a PCS.

Common Myths About Base Housing

Let’s clear a few things up.

  • “All base housing is outdated.” Not true. Many installations have fully renovated or brand-new homes.
  • “You lose money living on base.” Sometimes. Sometimes you save significantly.
  • “You have no choice.” You always have a choice—even if it doesn’t feel like it.

Understanding what is base housing today—not decades ago—changes the conversation.

Helpful Gear for Moving Into Base Housing

Base housing is usually unfurnished and comes with its own rules about nail holes, paint, and yard upkeep. A few practical items make the move-in smoother and help you pass the move-out inspection later:

  • Removable adhesive hooks and picture-hanging strips to decorate without nail holes
  • Blackout curtains and a tension curtain rod for rooms that only come with blinds
  • Cube storage organizers that adapt to any floor plan at your next PCS
  • Felt furniture pads to protect housing-issued floors
  • A basic home tool kit for reassembling furniture after the movers leave

For more ideas, see 8 renter-friendly upgrades to make base housing feel like home, and use our move-in and move-out inspection tips to protect yourself on day one. Planning your move? Start with our PCS moving checklist and BAH explainer.

Final Thoughts: Is Base Housing Worth It?

So, what is base housing really?

It’s a tool. A resource. A structured option designed to support military life—not define it.

For some families, it’s exactly what they need during a demanding assignment. For others, living off base offers freedom, savings, or space that better fits their season of life.

The key is clarity.
Know your priorities.
Run the numbers.
Ask the right questions.

And remember—housing should support your mission, not complicate it.

FAQs

1. What is base housing?

Base housing is residential housing located on or near a military installation for active-duty service members and their families.

2. Who qualifies for base housing?

Active-duty service members, especially those with dependents, typically qualify, with priority based on rank, family size, and availability.

3. Does base housing take all of my BAH?

In most cases, base housing uses 100% of your Basic Allowance for Housing as rent.

4. Are utilities included in base housing?

Yes, most base housing communities include utilities, though some may set usage caps.

5. Can I choose my specific home in base housing?

You usually cannot select a specific unit, but you may choose from available housing categories or neighborhoods.

6. Is base housing furnished?

Base housing is generally unfurnished, except for some overseas or temporary housing situations.

7. Are pets allowed in base housing?

Most base housing allows pets, but restrictions on number, size, or breed often apply.

8. How long are wait times for base housing?

Wait times vary by installation, season, and housing availability, ranging from immediate placement to several months.

9. Can I live off base instead of choosing base housing?

Yes, eligible service members may choose to live off base and use their BAH for civilian housing.

10. Is base housing a good option for long-term assignments?

It can be, especially for families who value stability and convenience, though off-base housing may offer more flexibility.

posts.title: Renting vs. Buying: What’s Best for Military Families?
posts.content:
Disclosure: Some links in this article are affiliate links. As an Amazon Associate, Military Housing Rentals earns from qualifying purchases, at no extra cost to you.

When it comes to military life, one thing is certain — change is constant. Orders drop. PCS moves happen. Duty stations shift. And with every new assignment comes a big question:

Should we rent or should we buy?

For many military families, this isn’t just a financial decision — it’s emotional, practical, and deeply personal. But let’s break it down with clarity. We’re not here to sugarcoat or overcomplicate it. We’re here to give you real, actionable advice — with an honest bias toward what works best for service members and their families.

Let’s talk about why military housing rentals often come out on top — and when buying might actually make sense.

Why Renting Often Wins for Military Families

Let’s face it. Military life doesn’t exactly scream “settled.” You’re likely to move every two to three years, and sometimes with short notice. In that kind of lifestyle, flexibility is gold.

1. You Can Move Without the Stress

PCS orders hit, and suddenly you’re looking at cross-country relocation. If you’re renting, it’s often as simple as giving notice and moving on. No open houses. No waiting for buyers. No worrying if the market’s in your favor.

And under the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act (SCRA), you can break your lease without penalty if you get reassigned. That’s a game-changer for military families.

2. No Risk of Being Stuck in a Bad Market

Buying a house in an unstable or overpriced market is a gamble — especially if you might have to sell in two years. If the market dips, you could end up upside down on your mortgage. Renting shields you from that risk. You’re not tied to resale values or fluctuating interest rates. You just pay the rent and go.

3. Zero Maintenance Costs

Hot water heater breaks? Landlord’s problem. Roof leaks? Call the property manager. When you’re renting, maintenance and repairs are someone else’s headache — not yours. That’s a huge relief, especially when you’re juggling deployments, long work hours, or being stationed overseas while your family holds things down at home.

4. Budgeting Is Easier With BAH

Your Basic Allowance for Housing (BAH) is meant to cover housing costs based on your rank and zip code. Most military rentals are priced with BAH in mind, so it’s easier to stay on budget. You don’t have to worry about hidden costs like property taxes, HOA dues, or surprise repairs eating into your paycheck.

The Case for Buying (And When It Makes Sense)

We’re not anti-buying. For some military families, homeownership does make sense — but only in very specific situations.

Here’s when buying might be a smart move:

1. You’re Stationed Long-Term

If you’re lucky enough to land a duty station where you’ll be for five years or more, buying can be a solid investment — especially if the local market is stable and appreciating. But remember, this is the exception, not the rule.

2. You Plan to Turn It Into a Rental

Some military homeowners turn their property into a rental when they PCS. That’s smart — if you’re ready to be a landlord or hire a property manager. But it comes with responsibilities, costs, and risks. Tenants. Vacancies. Repairs. Taxes. You have to be prepared.

3. You Have a Strong Financial Cushion

Buying isn’t just about the mortgage. You need savings for a down payment, closing costs, insurance, and emergencies. If you’re living paycheck-to-paycheck, buying can strain your finances — fast.

Let’s Talk Numbers: Renting vs. Buying

Let’s break it down with a quick example. Say your BAH is $2,000/month in your area.

  • Renting: You find a clean, modern home near base for $1,950/month. It includes lawn care, maintenance, and utilities.
  • Buying: You purchase a $250,000 home with a VA loan. Monthly mortgage + insurance + taxes = $1,850. Sounds good, right?

Now factor in:

  • Repairs: $300 for a busted AC
  • Moving early due to PCS: $8,000 in closing and realtor fees
  • Vacancy while you try to sell or rent it out

Suddenly, that monthly savings disappears — and your bank account feels the hit.

What Should Military Families Consider First?

Before you decide whether to rent or buy, ask yourself:

  1. How long will we be stationed here?
    • Less than 3 years? Rent.
  2. Can we handle sudden moves or deployments?
    • If you don’t want to manage a property from across the country, rent.
  3. Do we have savings for homeownership costs?
    • If not, renting protects your financial stability.
  4. Does the housing market support quick sales or rentals?
    • Not sure? Another reason to rent.

Common Misconceptions About Renting

Let’s clear the air on a few myths.

Renting is “throwing money away.”

Wrong. You’re paying for convenience, flexibility, and peace of mind — all of which are worth every penny in military life. Renting helps you avoid long-term financial risks and gives you breathing room when things change fast.

You’re not investing in your future.

Also wrong. Renting allows you to invest in your mobility, your family’s stability, and yes, even in the ability to save or invest elsewhere — like retirement accounts or stocks.

Tools That Make Renting Easier for Military Families

Renting keeps you flexible, and a little organization makes every PCS easier. These are practical, inexpensive items that help military renters stay on top of the move and protect their deposit:

  • A fireproof document bag for orders, leases, and inspection reports
  • A monthly budget planner to keep rent and utilities within your BAH
  • Heavy-duty moving boxes and packing tape for a personally procured move
  • A magic eraser sponge pack and spackle repair kit for move-out touch-ups

Before you sign your next lease, read how the SCRA lets you break a lease on PCS orders and how BAH works. Looking off base? Our guide to finding off-base housing near your duty station covers scams to avoid and questions to ask.

Final Verdict: Renting is Built for Military Life

Owning a home can be a smart long-term strategy — but only when your situation supports it.

For most military families, renting is the clear winner. It gives you control over your finances, flexibility during PCS moves, and freedom from stress when duty calls. And in today’s housing market? That’s not just smart — it’s survival.

If you’re navigating a move or searching for your next home near base, focus on what matters: safety, affordability, and flexibility. And that’s exactly what military housing rentals are designed to offer.

Ready to Find Your Next Rental?

At MilitaryHousingRentals.com, we make it easy to search military-friendly listings near your base. Whether you’re stationed stateside or preparing for your next PCS, we’ve got the tools and support to help you find the right home — fast.

Browse properties by base, and connect with landlords who understand your lifestyle.

Your mission is service. Ours is helping you find a place to call home — no matter where duty takes you.

props.title: McGraw Village – Heritage Landing at Fort Benning
props.content:
McGraw Village is a family housing neighborhood at Fort Benning, Georgia (called Fort Moore from 2023 to 2025), managed by The Michaels Organization as part of Heritage Landing. The neighborhood offers single-family homes and duplexes for senior noncommissioned officers in the ranks of E6-E8.

Homes feature two-car garages and backyards on sidewalk-lined streets. A popular floor plan, the Mourning Dove, offers three bedrooms, two-and-a-half baths, and about 1,720 square feet. Accessible floor plans are also available.

McGraw Village is steps from McBride Elementary School and the child development center. The village center has a large pool, splash ground, and community center, and there is a dog park for four-legged family members. Heritage Landing has two- to five-bedroom homes across Fort Benning, so contact the Family Housing Welcome Center for current availability.

props.title: Dakota Ridge – Fort Carson Family Homes
props.content:
Dakota Ridge is a family housing neighborhood at Fort Carson, Colorado, just south of Colorado Springs, managed by Balfour Beatty Communities as part of Fort Carson Family Homes. The neighborhood offers four-bedroom homes for noncommissioned officers in the ranks of E5-E6.

Homes feature open floor plans, fully equipped kitchens, garages, patios, and fenced backyards, along with ceiling fans, central air, and washer and dryer hookups. With Pikes Peak views and easy access to the outdoors, it is a great fit for active families.

Dakota Ridge is near Patriot Elementary School, Carson Middle School, and Cheyenne Shadows Golf Club. Fort Carson Family Homes neighborhoods include playgrounds, athletic courts, trails, and community gardens, and they are pet friendly. Contact the leasing office for current availability.

props.title: Stuart Mesa – Liberty Military Housing
props.content:
Stuart Mesa is a military family housing community at Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton in Oceanside, California, managed by Liberty Military Housing. It sits near Del Mar Beach and is close to the Marine Corps Exchange and Carlsbad Premium Outlets, with restaurants and shops within walking distance.

The community offers two- to five-bedroom townhomes ranging from about 1,251 to 1,971 square feet, such as a three-bedroom, two-and-a-half-bath plan of about 1,377 square feet. Features include private patios, vaulted ceilings, walk-in closets, ceiling fans, and washer and dryer hookups, and garages are available.

Stuart Mesa has some of the best amenities on base: a community pool, fitness center, three dog parks, 20 playgrounds and tot lots, nine basketball courts, a soccer field, BBQ and picnic areas, plus free community events and 24/7 maintenance. Contact Liberty Military Housing for current availability and eligibility.

props.title: SP Enlist – Naval Station Norfolk
props.content:
SP Enlist is an on-base military housing community at Naval Station Norfolk, Virginia, managed by Liberty Military Housing. Living inside the gates puts you close to the piers, the commissary, and the exchange at the world’s largest naval station.

The community offers four-bedroom, two-and-a-half-bath townhomes of about 1,405 square feet. Homes feature a fully equipped kitchen with stainless-steel appliances, a detached one-car garage, a fenced rear yard, air conditioning, and carpet throughout.

Residents enjoy on-base gated entry, a playground, basketball courts, and Liberty’s Little Libraries. Liberty manages more than 1,600 homes across ten communities in the Norfolk and Hampton Roads area and does not require credit checks or deposits for active-duty members. Contact Liberty Military Housing for current availability.

props.title: Gardner Hills – Campbell Crossing
props.content:
Gardner Hills is a family housing neighborhood in The Woodlands area of Fort Campbell, Kentucky, near Gate 1. It is part of Campbell Crossing, the Army’s privatized housing partnership on post, which has more than 4,000 homes across four communities. Different phases of Gardner Hills are designated for junior and senior noncommissioned officers.

A typical floor plan, The Lydia, offers three bedrooms and about 1,632 square feet, with a kitchen open to the dining room, a primary suite with a private bath, a one-car garage, and a fenced yard. Residents get complimentary front and side lawn service, free 24/7 on-site maintenance, and access to a Home and Garden Self Help Center.

Gardner Hills residents are served by The Commons at the Woodlands, with a meeting room and full kitchen, fitness room, splash park, walking trails, playgrounds, and tennis courts. Schools, a shoppette, and a coffee shop are nearby. Campbell Crossing is pet friendly (with breed restrictions) and is open to active duty, retirees, DoD civilians, and contractors. Contact the leasing office for availability.

props.title: Meriwether Landing – Liberty Military Housing
props.content:
Meriwether Landing is one of the newest military housing communities at Joint Base Lewis-McChord, Washington. It opened on Lewis North in 2025 and is managed by Liberty Military Housing. The neighborhood has more than 200 new-construction duplex and single-family homes near American Lake and Meriwether Elementary School.

Floor plans are assigned by rank. For example, a two-story duplex for E5-E9 families has four bedrooms, two-and-a-half baths, and about 1,977 square feet, while officer and senior enlisted plans range up to about 2,500 square feet. Homes include attached two-car garages, fenced backyards, private patios, laundry rooms, air conditioning, pantries, walk-in closets, and modern flooring.

Residents are close to five parks with playgrounds and have access to community center amenities, Liberty’s Little Libraries, and free monthly resident events. The community is pet friendly, allowing up to four pets with some breed restrictions. Visit Liberty Military Housing’s website for current availability.

props.title: Tarawa Terrace II – Camp Lejeune Family Housing
props.content:
Tarawa Terrace II is a large family housing neighborhood just inside the Wilson Gate at Marine Corps Base Camp Lejeune, North Carolina, off Bougainville Drive. Named for the World War II Marine Corps battle in the Gilbert Islands, the neighborhood is managed by Hunt Military Communities and includes 778 two-, three-, and four-bedroom townhomes.

Floor plans include a three-bedroom, two-and-a-half-bath layout of about 1,618 square feet. Homes include screened patios, programmable thermostats, a dishwasher, garbage disposal, and microwave, walk-in closets and extra storage, air conditioning, and washer and dryer hookups. Select homes have fenced backyards or fireplaces.

Tarawa Terrace II is open to E1-E5 active-duty Marines and Sailors and may also be available to retirees and people who work on the installation. Residents benefit from professional landscaping, on-site management, 24-hour emergency maintenance, and nearby parks and playgrounds. Contact Camp Lejeune Family Housing for current availability.

props.title: Nijmegen – Corvias at Fort Bragg
props.content:
Nijmegen is an on-post family housing neighborhood at Fort Bragg, North Carolina (called Fort Liberty from 2023 to 2025), managed by Corvias. The neighborhood offers three- and four-bedroom duplexes and townhomes with two to two-and-a-half baths, ranging from roughly 1,269 to 1,985 square feet depending on the floor plan.

All homes include washer and dryer hookups, and many have garages and outdoor storage. Select ADA-compliant homes are available. Nijmegen sits just off Longstreet Road with quick access to the 82nd Airborne Division area, and it is less than five minutes from the South Post Commissary and Exchange.

The Nijmegen Community Center has a fitness room for residents, and the neighborhood is near an elementary school and a dog park. Corvias also offers resort-style pools, basketball courts, playgrounds, and multimedia rooms across Fort Bragg. Contact Corvias for current availability and rank eligibility.

props.title: George Moore Park – Fort Bliss Family Homes
props.content:
George Moore Park is a family housing neighborhood on Fort Bliss in El Paso, Texas, managed by Balfour Beatty Communities as part of Fort Bliss Family Homes. It is designed for junior enlisted Soldiers (E1-E6) and their families, with two- and three-bedroom homes that have one to two baths.

The neighborhood’s biggest draw is its location. It is within walking distance of Logan Elementary School, the George Underwood Golf Course, and several shops and restaurants, so many errands can be done without getting in the car.

Residents enjoy Fort Bliss Family Homes’ pet-friendly communities, with pools, playgrounds, park areas, and sport courts across post. George Moore Park is one of 17 Fort Bliss Family Homes neighborhoods. Call the leasing office for current floor plans and availability.

props.title: Randolph Family Housing – JBSA-Randolph
props.content:
Randolph Family Housing offers historic homes inside the gates of JBSA-Randolph, the famous “Showplace of the Air Force” in Universal City, just northeast of San Antonio. Managed by Hunt Military Communities, the neighborhood is known for its stucco exteriors, original hardwood floors, and Spanish Colonial Revival character, with homes renovated since 2007.

Most homes have four bedrooms, and some plans have five. The operator lists dozens of floor plans, such as a four-bedroom, three-bath layout of about 2,187 square feet. Features vary by home and include central air, Energy Star appliances, decorative fireplaces, patios, private backyards in select homes, and carport-style carriage houses.

The gated, walkable community includes a pool, fitness center, community center, parks, and playgrounds, and trash, recycling, and bulk pickup are included. Housing is open to active duty across enlisted and officer ranks, and may also be available to retirees, DoD civilians, and Guard and Reserve members. Contact the leasing office for current availability.

meta.address: 205 New B St E, Universal City, TX 78148

props.title: Watkins Terrace – Fort Sam Houston Family Housing
props.content:
Watkins Terrace is a family housing neighborhood at JBSA-Fort Sam Houston in San Antonio, managed by Hunt Military Communities. The neighborhood offers single-story and two-story three- and four-bedroom homes, with three-bedroom plans of about 1,200 square feet and four-bedroom plans of about 1,380 square feet.

Homes feature central air conditioning, washer and dryer hookups, and attached garages. Watkins Terrace is close to the on-post child development center, the elementary and high schools, and the MWR sports field, which makes daily routines easy for families with children. Pets are welcome, with breed and size restrictions.

Residents have access to Fort Sam Houston’s community amenities, including three community pools, 16 playgrounds, basketball and tennis courts, walking trails, a self-help store, and 24-hour emergency maintenance. Active-duty families pay rent in arrears with no up-front rent or security deposit. Contact the housing office for current availability and rank eligibility.

props.title: Heritage Heights – Cavalry Family Housing
props.content:
Heritage Heights is one of the newest on-post neighborhoods at Fort Hood (known as Fort Cavazos from 2023 to 2025), built for junior enlisted Soldiers and their families. The neighborhood replaces the 1960s-era Chaffee Village, which began coming down in 2021, and is managed by Cavalry Family Housing, the Army’s privatized housing partner on post.

Homes are single-family three-bedroom, two-bath designs with open floor plans, gathering spaces, and two-car garages. They are Energy Star certified and built to LEED design standards, so they run efficiently and stay comfortable through Central Texas summers. Hundreds of homes were completed in 2024, and more are planned through 2027.

Outside your door you will find walking paths, community gardens, a dog park, and a playground. Cavalry Family Housing operates 11 neighborhoods on post, so contact the leasing office or visit their website for current availability, eligibility, and floor plan details.

meta.address: 18010 T.J. Mills Blvd Ste B209, Fort Hood, TX 76544

props.title: Airman Scott Village 1193 – Lackland Family Homes
props.content:
Airman Scott Village 1193 is a spacious two-bedroom, one-bath home located within the secure, gated community of Lackland Family Homes on Lackland Air Force Base in San Antonio. This residence offers military families the comfort and convenience of living on base with the added benefits of a walkable neighborhood and a strong sense of community. It’s an ideal housing option for active-duty service members stationed at Lackland AFB.

The 1,193 sq. ft. floor plan features updated finishes, a fully equipped kitchen, and garage access—perfect for families who need functional space and modern features. Designed with military life in mind, this home includes curbside trash service, lawn care, and on-site maintenance to take the stress out of home upkeep. Pet-friendly policies and lighted walking trails make this a great place for the whole family, pets included.

Residents enjoy access to a wide range of community amenities, including pools, playgrounds, picnic areas, basketball and tennis courts, a sand volleyball court, and a community center that regularly hosts resident events. With all of Lackland AFB’s facilities nearby, including schools, commissary, and medical services, Airman Scott Village 1193 offers everything a military household needs in one connected and supportive environment.

meta.address: 2254 Brian Mcelroy Dr, San Antonio, TX 78236

props.title: Comanche – Cavalry Family Housing
props.content:
Comanche I is a dedicated military housing community offering comfortable two-bedroom, one-bath homes located right on Fort Cavazos. Ideal for active-duty service members and their families, this small, quiet neighborhood provides the convenience of on-post living with easy access to major roads like Clear Creek and Tank Destroyer. Its single-story layout and recent upgrades to windows, doors, and exterior siding ensure both comfort and modern appeal.

These homes come fully equipped with all major appliances, washer/dryer connections, central air conditioning, and newly installed privacy fencing. All utilities are included, giving military families one less thing to worry about when budgeting. Mature trees provide shade throughout the community, and added touches like a little free library help foster a friendly, close-knit atmosphere.

Residents enjoy close proximity to key Fort Cavazos amenities including the PX, Commissary, Furniture Store, golf course, and recreation centers. With walking trails, basketball and tennis courts, and multiple playgrounds nearby, Comanche I offers the perfect mix of convenience and quality of life for those who serve.
